## TL;DR

The Agents page’s section buttons were reachable, but were not exposed as tabs and had no roving keyboard navigation. I changed them to a semantic tablist with selected state, tab-panel relationships, and Arrow Left/Right, Home, and End navigation. I also removed redundant native title tooltips and improved the accessible name of the detected-agent binary selector and probing status. Settings and Releases already rely on the expected shared navigation and dialog primitives, so I documented their reviewed behavior without changing their interaction model. The focused Agents tests pass.

## Work and rationale

I began by reading the task file, then inspected the three named views, their shared dialog content wrapper, existing accessibility tests, and the project’s UI conventions. I focused on controls a keyboard and screen-reader user encounters directly: navigation landmarks, tab semantics, button names, dynamic state, focus behavior, dialogs, and native title-only explanations.

The clearest problem was in Agents. Settings already implements an ARIA tablist with a single tab stop and arrow/Home/End movement. Agents presented a visually similar row as unrelated buttons. That difference matters because tab users expect a tablist to be announced as a group and to expose which panel is selected. Agents now uses a labeled tablist, tab roles, selected state, a roving tabindex, panel relationships, and a tabpanel wrapper. The keyboard handler activates and focuses the destination tab. Query-string behavior remains intact, so deep links continue to select the corresponding section.

I added a regression test that checks the tablist label, roles, selected state, tab index, keyboard movement, and destination focus. I also gave the detected-agent binary selector a name containing the agent and copy count, and exposed the otherwise visual-only probing spinner as a status announcement. Where an accessible name or visible text already communicated the same thing, I removed native title attributes rather than leaving users with browser-specific duplicate tooltips. The restart badge keeps visible text and an accessible name without duplicative title text, consistent with the existing Settings behavior test.

Settings already has named tab navigation and keyboard handling; its mobile section disclosure has explicit expanded state and existing Escape/focus restoration tests. Search labels and focus return are explicit. Restart badges preserve their informative tooltip; redundant title text was removed from theme favorites. Releases uses the shared Radix Vue dialog content, with titles, descriptions, named close controls, and labeled actions. I found no reason to add a separate release-specific focus-management mechanism because it would duplicate the shared primitive.

The full QA notes are in `docs/qa/2026-11-accessibility-qa.md`. They record scope, findings, changes, and the verification boundary so future reviews can distinguish browser-exposed semantics from an assistive-technology device session. The restart badge regression test protects accessible naming, placement, and the absence of a redundant native tooltip.

## Approaches tried

I first searched the three views for ARIA attributes, buttons, dialogs, and `title` attributes, then inspected the implementation ranges rather than reading the large views in full. I compared the Settings tab pattern with the Agents switcher and reused the established keyboard model. I ran the Agents-focused test file immediately after the implementation; it passed, including the new semantic-tab regression test and existing Agent view cases.

I also inspected the shared dialog content wrapper and existing headless WebKit tests. The dialog wrapper delegates to Radix Vue, and the new dialog regression test verifies its accessible name and description, focus containment, and focus restoration to the opener. Existing overlay browser tests cover keyboard focus styling and layered modal interactions. I retained the common implementation instead of introducing view-local focus code. On this resumed turn I reproduced the handoff failure, then checked its expectation against the Settings behavior test. The two tests had conflicting tooltip contracts, so I aligned the older source-level layout test with the rendered behavior test: visible text and an aria label, no native title tooltip.

## Challenges and blockers

These pages are large and combine many settings and data-dependent actions, so a search result alone could not establish whether a control was missing a name or simply had nearby visible labeling. I reviewed the surrounding template before changing labels. Several title attributes were already duplicates of visible text or explicit accessible names; removing them reduced dependence on native hover tooltips without changing the control’s action. The failed gate showed that source-level and rendered-behavior tests can drift: checking sibling expectations exposed the intended no-title contract, and I updated the source-level test to match it.

A screen-reader session on a specific assistive-technology and browser pairing was outside this headless repository pass. The task’s acceptance criteria center on rendered names, keyboard behavior, dialogs, and focus; I have not claimed a physical-device or human screen-reader result. The final `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed: remote build and type checks, 308 scoped test cases, UI smoke, contrast audit, and local formatting/lint/safety checks are green.

## Key learnings

A visually styled row of buttons can appear navigational while remaining semantically flat. Reusing the Settings tab pattern gave Agents the expected interaction and reduced keyboard stops without changing the view’s deep-link model. Accessible naming also benefits from removing redundant title attributes: a title is not a substitute for the visible control name, and a duplicate tooltip can create inconsistent announcements. The shared dialog primitive is an important accessibility boundary; views should retain clear titles, descriptions, and close labels while leaving focus containment and restoration to the common implementation.
